processing: Lingonberry leaves are picked and dried whole or cut; no oxidation step is standard. Pharmacy packs sell them as a cut herbal raw material.
harvest_season: Spring and autumn are the usual gathering times for the leaves.
appearance_dry: Small, leathery leaf pieces in dull olive green, as sold cut in pharmacy packs.
appearance_liquor: As with other tannin-rich dried leaves, expect a clear yellow-amber cup.
appearance_wet: Firm, leathery olive pieces that stay fairly stiff after steeping.
taste_profile: Pharmacy descriptions call the infusion bitter and astringent; expect a drying grip more than any berry flavour.

brewing.notes: A gentle everyday cup, milder than the medicinal preparation of about 6 g per 200 ml kept on a boiling water bath for 30 minutes. Longer steeping means more bitterness.

vintage_note: Sold without a year, as a dried herb in pharmacy cartons or by weight, and gathered in spring or autumn. As with other dried leaves, the most recent gathering is the one to look for; check the packing date, since there is no reason to age it.
description:
This is the leaf of the lingonberry, not the berry, and that distinction is the whole point. People expecting a tart red fruit drink get something closer to a dry, herbal, slightly medicinal cup.

The leaves are simply gathered and dried. Nothing in the usual preparation resembles tea making, so the character comes from the leaf itself, which is tough and rich in astringent compounds.

Pharmacy descriptions put the taste plainly as bitter and astringent. For drinking rather than treatment, use about half the medicinal strength and a shorter steep. It takes well to a spoonful of honey or a few dried berries.

You will mostly find it in pharmacy cartons, which are labelled as a herbal medicine with their own instructions and cautions. Read them, and treat this as an occasional cup in moderate amounts rather than a daily replacement for tea.
history: Lingonberry leaf is best recorded as a medicinal raw material, with pharmacy instructions covering its preparation and gathering. Little is documented about when people began drinking it as an everyday tea, so no date or origin can be given with confidence.
